Social Class and Ethnic Issues in Making Drugs Illegal
 • There were real concerns related to health
   safety, but many of the early legislation of
  nonmedical drug use was driven by class,
   race, and ethnic concerns

      • Prohibition of alcohol was in part a response to the
       drinking practices of European immigrants (the
      new lower class)
      • Cocaine became illegal after it was associated with
       African Americans following Reconstruction
      • Opium was first restricted in California in 1875
      CE, when it became synonymous with Chinese
       immigrant workers
      • Marijuana was legal until the 1930s CE, when it
      became associated with Mexican immigrant
       workers
      • LSD, legal in the 1950s, became illegal in 1967
      when it became associated with the counterculture

Creation of the DEA

• The United States Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) was
  enacted on 1 July 1973

• The purpose behind the creation of the DEA –
       •  Enforce the controlled substances laws and regulations of the United States

       •  Bring to the criminal and civil justice system of the United States, or any competent
          jurisdiction, organizations and their principal members involved in the growing,
         manufacture, or distribution of controlled substances appearing, in or destined for,
             illicit traffic in the United Sates

       •  Recommend and support non-enforcement programs aimed at reducing availability
         of illicit controlled substances

• The DEA was created to consolidate and coordinate the government’s
  drug control activities

Penalties and Sentencing

                                        •  Legal repercussions – people caught engaging in illegal
                                   behaviors involving drugs face a variety of consequences,
                                     including:
                                               •  Time in jail or federal prison
                                               • Heavy fines
                                               • Community service
                                               •  Probation
                                               •  Other forms of confinement like house arrest
                                               •  Criminal record that affects one's ability to get or
                                        maintain a job, receive approval for college loans,
                                            vote, own a gun, or join the military

                                        • The penalties for drug-related charges are determined by
                                      several factors:
                                               •  Substance
                                               • Amount of substance
                                               •  Activity the individual was engaged in
                                               •  Prior encounters with law enforcement

                                        •  Individuals committing serious crimes with large amounts
                                    of dangerous drugs are more likely to receive harsher
                                       penalties

• Manufacture – production of an illegal

Distribution


• Distribution – sale, transfer, exchange,
  import, or export of a controlled substance
  from one individual to another

•  Distribution of drugs covers a variety of
   illegal activities including, but not limited
   to:
      • Shipping drugs via mail
      •  Transporting drugs via car, boat, plane,
       skateboard, scooter, or other mode of
        transportation
      •  Selling drugs to another
      • Giving drugs to another
      •  Advertising the sale of drugs
      • Coordinating the transport or sale of
       drugs




                                                                                                   RXRS-201 | T.D. Church | 2026

Distribution

                                                        •  Distribution is further defined as -

                                                              • Actual Distribution – when one
                                                   person physically transfers the
                                                       controlled substance to another

                                                              • Constructive Distribution– intent to
                                                                 sell or distribute illegal substances
                                                   through one’s actions or the quantity of
                                                   drugs in their possession
                                                                   • A large quantity of drugs,
                                                           baggies, and a scale infers that the
                                                       drugs are being “packaged to
                                                                   sell” rather than for personal use

                                                              • Attempted Distribution – when an
                                                       individual attempts to transfer the
                                                       controlled substance to another, but is
                                                    otherwise prevented from doing so

Social Impacts



                                                                               •  Although narcotics are illegal in the United States, they
                                                               are seen as a recreational activity by different
                                                             populations

                                                                               •   Illicit drugs are a commodity with strong demand,
                                                                     resulting in their sales at a higher price

                                                                                       •  This high price is due to several factors that
                                                                        include:
                                                                                               •  Potential legal ramifications
                                                                                               •  Potential for violence from other dealers
                                                               and buyers
                                                                                               •  Importation and transportation
                                                                                               •  Processing and storage

                                                                               •  Media and politicians have helped to entrench and
                                                                  continually renew constructs of illicit drug use as
                                                        immoral

                                                                                       •  Abstinence from drugs and alcohol is seen as the
                                                                     morally and socially correct path for citizens to
                                                                        follow

Four Geographical Features of
Open Air Drug Markets



Open-air drug markets are often located in inner city
or urban areas, with the following common features:

 1. Located in economically depressed
   neighborhoods

 2. Dealers sell from static sites so customers know
   where to find them

 3. Typically located near a transportation hub where
    there is a level of legitimate activity

 4. Markets have a reputation for selling drugs and
   can grow large in size, the concentration of
    activity in a small area will be hard to disguise

theories For and Against Legalization
Area of Effect          Rationale
Legal risk                           •  The risk of arrest increases the expected cost of obtaining and using a prohibited
                                   substance
Stigma                               •  A change in the legal risk could also affect the stigma associated with the activity
                                       •   User’s family and friends may be more accepting of marijuana use and home
                                   production if they know the state no longer prohibits these activities
                                       •   Medicalization reduces the belief that consumption is harmful
Forbidden fruit                    •  Some people may find marijuana more attractive to use because it is illegal and
                                   perceived as dangerous
                                       •   Medicalization could be seen as mainstreaming the activity, making it less
                                         attractive for some individuals
Availability                         •   Variation in how marijuana laws are implemented in the U.S.
                                       •  Most states allow for dispensaries (stores that sell only marijuana products), but the
                                          ratio of dispensaries to patients varies dramatically
                                       •   This can reduce the search costs for obtaining marijuana and can also increase
                                    access to a variety of marijuana products
Promotion                          •   Physical stores can serve as advertisements
                                       •   Marketing of marijuana products is loosely regulated and ads can be found in news
                                     weeklies, on billboards, and the internet
                                       •   In Los Angeles, the level of exposure to marijuana advertising has been associated
                                  with a greater propensity to use marijuana
Price                                 •  A large portion of what users spend on illegal drugs is sued to compensate the
                                      dealer and everyone else along the supply line chain for their risk of arrest,
                                       incarceration, and violence  RXRS-201 | T.D. Church | 2026

Potency Problems

•  Marijuana was named a Schedule 1 drug in 1970 and the only source
    for US testing was from a single strain under the control of the
   National Center for Natural Projects Research (NCNPR) at the
   University of Mississippi (Oxford, MS)

        •  1970s – 90% of all recreational marijuana was imported
           illegally (predominately Colombia)

        •  Due to growing time, transportation, and distribution methods,
            this marijuana was not always ideal, contained very little of the
         feminized flower (sinsemilla), and contained much more
          “additive” materials (stems, seeds, etc)

        •  1980s – the first hydroponic systems were introduced, and
        homegrown marijuana began to be sold

text:
Drinking Patterns as Signs of Alcohol Problems

1.Lying About or Hiding Your Drinking – Denial is common with people having
problems with alcohol, so both problem drinkers and alcoholics might drink
secretively or lie about how much they drink to make it seem like less of an issue.
This can be hard to spot for anybody but the individual, due to its very nature, but it’s
an important sign of a more serious problem.
2.Drinking to Relax or Feel Better – Almost all people struggling with addiction
abuse their substance of choice for emotional reasons. Whether it’s stress,
depression, anxiety or anything else, using alcohol as a method of easing negative
feelings is a risky habit—the “relief” it provides is only temporary and it ordinarily
makes things worse in the long run. If you drink more when you’ve had a stressful
day or need a drink to feel like you can really relax, it’s a big sign that you’re using
alcohol as an emotional crutch.
3.“Blacking Out” Regularly – Drinking so much that you have no memory of what
happened is another red flag for a problem with alcohol. Simply put, it means you
drank way too much. If you find this happening to you (or notice it happening to
someone else), you have to ask what is driving you to drink so excessively? You
don’t need to black out to have fun, so what’s the real reason?
4.Being Unable to Stop Once You Start – If you always finish a bottle of wine once
it’s opened or drink all the beer in the house once you’ve had one, it’s another sign
you aren’t in full control of your drinking and you may have a problem.

                                         Spring 2026        Pharmacy Undergraduate Programs

deck_name: Week 15 Davies Alcohol Addiction FN FAll 2025.pdf
text:
Signs of Alcohol Problems

5.Drinking in Dangerous Situations – Drinking when you really shouldn’t—like
before work, before you have to drive somewhere or drinking against your doctor’s
orders when you’re on medication—is an important sign of problem drinking. Even if
something hasn’t gone wrong yet, every time you do something like this you run the
risk of serious consequences. Regularly taking those risks strongly implies that
alcohol is the main priority in your life.

6.Neglecting Your Responsibilities – If you’re having problems at work, school or
with your household responsibilities because of your drinking, you have a problem.
Alcohol has crossed the line from an occasional indulgence to something that
seriously impacts your day-to-day functioning.

7.Having Trouble in Your Relationships – This is closely related to the last point,
but it’s in many ways more important. If your drinking is causing problems with your
closest friends, your significant other or your family, it’s an indication that alcohol is a
bigger priority than even the most important people in your life. These last two
symptoms are general signs of any addiction, and might mean that your issues are
going beyond the problem-drinker stage.


                                          Spring 2026        Pharmacy Undergraduate Programs

deck_name: Week 15 Davies Alcohol Addiction FN FAll 2025.pdf
text:
Signs of Alcohol Problems

8.Being Able to Drink More Than You Used To – Tolerance is another key sign of
addiction, so if you can drink more than you used to and need to drink more than you
did before in order to get drunk, it’s a strong indicator that you’re becoming an
alcoholic. It means your body is exposed to alcohol regularly enough that it has
adapted to cope with it better.

9.Trying to Quit but Being Unable to – If you have realized your drinking is
becoming a problem (or someone who cares about you has) and tried to make a
change but have been unsuccessful, you should seriously consider finding additional
help. Deciding to quit drinking shows that you understand the impacts it’s having on
your life, but the fact that you’re unable to means there’s a big chance you’re
struggling with alcohol addiction.

10.Experiencing Withdrawal – Withdrawal is different from a hangover; it’s the
reaction to the lack of alcohol rather than too much alcohol. If you start to feel
irritable, tired, depressed, nauseous or anxious when you haven’t had a drink,
there’s a possibility you’re going through withdrawal. Other signs include having
trouble sleeping, losing your appetite and experiencing shakiness or trembling.

Bioterrorism Categories
•  Bioterrorism – the deliberate release of viruses,
   bacteria, or other germs (agents) used to cause illness or
  death in people, animals, or plants

   •  These biological agents are classified into three categories:

   •  Category A – agents can be easily disseminated or
      transmitted from person to person
        •  Result in high mortality rates and have the potential for major
          public health impact
        •  May cause public panic and social disruption, and require special
          action for public health preparedness

   •  Category B – agents that are moderately easy to disseminate
        •  Result in moderate morbidity rates and low mortality, and require
           specific enhanced diagnostic capacity and disease surveillance

   •  Category C – emerging agents that could be engineered for
     mass dissemination in the future because of their availability
        •  Easy to produce and disseminate
        •   Potentially linked to high morbidity and mortality rates, and major
          health impact

Detecting Pain: Major Points
•Nociception is the form of somatic sensation that detects noxious, potentially tissue-damaging stimuli.
 •Pain has both a localizing somatic sensory component and an aversive emotional and motivational component.
•Pain begins with peripheral nociceptors, cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of body and trigeminal ganglia in the head.
 •Peripheral nociceptors express a set of channels, called transient receptor potential (TRP) channels sensitive to noxious
mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli.
 •  These neurons also express receptors for inflammatory mediators and substances released by damaged cells.

Evolution of Nociception
and Survival

Sensitization of Tissue





•  A burn or sting produces an area of reddening or flare that extends beyond the injury
•  An even larger area is characterized by enhanced sensitivity to subsequent stimulation, which reflects the sensitization of
   nociceptive neurons.
•  Previously innocuous stimuli, such as light touch, now activate nociceptors and are experienced as painful; termed
   allodynia (decreased threshold).

Neurogenic Inflammation

•  Neurogenic inflammation: release of peptides at peripheral terminals of nociceptive neurons into surrounding tissues.
•  Bidirection flow of information between the nervous system and immune system.
•  “Retrograde” release occurs in response to tissue damage, endogenous inflammatory mediators, or exogenous chemicals.
•  Neurogenic inflammation is a normal homeostatic response to inflammation or tissue damage in diverse organs,
   including skin, joints, gut, and respiratory system.
•  Inappropriate or excessive immune response can contribute to pathological conditions, including arthritis, diabetes, and
  asthma or other autoimmune disorders.

Neuropathic Pain

Damage (cutting, compression, injury, disease) of neurons in nociceptive pathways generally causes some loss of normal
pain sensation. After a delay, damage can result in continuous prolonged neuropathic pain.

➢Compared to other chemicals in the18th century, opium was a benign

➢Opium was prescribed for rheumatism and insomnia.

Treating Psychosis
➢During the 18th century, opium was found to be a good remedy for nervous disorders.
➢Due to its sedative and tranquilizing properties, it was used to quiet the minds of those with psychosis, help with
   people who were considered insane, and to help treat patients with insomnia.
➢Despite its medicinal values, it was noted that in cases of psychosis, it could cause anger or depression, and due to
   the drug's euphoric effects, it could cause depressed patients to become more depressed after the effects wore off
   because they would get used to being high (the new normal)

Opium and Literature
➢Thomas de Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1822), one of the first literary accounts

Medical Examiners vs Coroners: Both investigate all unnatural,
   sudden, unexpected, unexplained or unattended deaths.
   Testing for the presence of potential poisons in deceased persons

However, they differ in their legal power in the Court of Law:

Coroners: position created in Britain; 900 AD
  No degree/training required!
  Have a quasi-judicial role: hold and preside over inquiries.

Medical examiners: position created in Boston; 1877
  Must be physician.
  Do not have the judicial powers of Coroner
   Usually called to appear as a witness.

The historical poison: ARSENIC = “inheritance powder”
● Naturally found in ores with copper, gold, lead, zinc as sulfides minerals:
     realgar (red), orpiment (yellow-orange)

● In ancient times, used in paints, inks, dyes, but recognized
    as poison/medication in ancient Greece and Rome

● In the Middle Ages & Renaissance, used for familial and
     political poisonings: in 1600s-1700s France, called “poudre de succession”

● Until 1900s, would-be poisoners could easy get Arsenic:
    used in insecticides, weed killers, rat poison, cosmetics!
● Also found as environmental pollutant: ground water, smelter,
         cigarette smoke, agriculture runoffs
● Medical uses (from 2,400 years ago by Hippocrates)
   Older uses: anti-ulcer, antispasmodic, antiseptic
   More recent: anti-syphilitic, psoriasis treatment
   New uses: analogs may have anti-leukemic action

History of Modern Forsensic Toxicology
 How Arsenic poisoning and the development of the Marsh Test gave the
             impetus needed to validate forensic toxicology
● JAMES MARSH (1836):
    sensitive method to detect Arsenic (10 μg) in tissues
   ● Sample suspected to contain As (food, tissues, body fluid…)
   + zinc + Acid (hydrochloric/sulfuric) → arsine gas (AsH3) (garlic smell)
    Arsine gas + heat → water vapor + arsenic powder
                     (black & shiny deposit: arsenic mirror)

               ● Few years later, Orfila validated
                        the use of Marsh's test as
                           forensic evidence in trial
                  Marsh Test became the standard for 100 yrs

New forensic findings on Medici Poisonings

“When a Medici dies, the first assumption is arsenic” (R. J. Hamilton, medical toxicologist; Drexel U)

•  Poisoning case: deaths of Francesco de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany
  and his wife Bianca Cappello 1587

      (liver samples) found in broken terra-cotta jar.

Seven New Definitions
• By 1880 CE seven categories of mental illness were suggested by
 US medical schools:

     • Mania – excitement manifested by mental and physical hyperactivity,
       disorganization of behavior, and elevation of mood
     • Melancholia – condition characterized by extreme depression, bodily
      complaints, and often hallucinations and delusions
     • Monomania – excessive concentration on a single object or idea
     • Paresis – slight or partial paralysis; characterized by memory loss, muscle
      weakness, progressive dementia, and seizures
     • Dementia – development of multiple cognitive deficits such as memory
      impairment, aphasia, and the inability to plan and initiate complex behavior
     • Dipsomania – uncontrollable craving for alcoholic beverages; chronic
       addiction
     • Epilepsy - abnormal electrical discharges in the brain and typically manifested
     by sudden brief episodes of altered or diminished consciousness, involuntary
      movements, or convulsions

       •  Treatment planning – one of the main purposes of diagnosis is to guide treatment planning
                 •  A systematic catalog of diagnoses is useful, because it helps health professionals know that a disorder has shown to be

                 •  The best evidence-based practice can be applied to a newly diagnosed disorder
       •  The diagnosis also aids in establishing a prognosis for the patient, and enables communication among
         professionals involved in the patient’s care
• Evidence-Based Practice – refers to any concept or strategy that is derived from or informed
  by objective evidence such as research and scientific studies as a base for determining the

   (Germany)
    •   Sweet-smelling, colorless liquid used as a
       solvent and general anesthetic

    •  Chloroform is typically created through the
       action of chlorine bleach powder (calcium

       ethanol (generic process known as haloform
        reaction)

Sedation by Ether
•  October 16, 1846 - crowd of doctors and students in the
   surgical amphitheater at Massachusetts General Hospital
   looked on as a dentist named William T.G.
  Morton instructed a patient to inhale the fumes from an
   ether-soaked sponge
   •  After the patient was sufficiently sedated, a surgeon
     removed a tumor from his neck

   • When the patient awoke from his ether-induced
      stupor, the surgeon asked how he felt, to which he
      reportedly replied, “feels as if my neck’s been
      scratched”

     seemed like a miracle at the time

   •  Ether obviously made surgery a more comfortable

      take their time operating on anesthetized patients,

     more complex and beneficial surgical techniques
